control.description: The unmodified target revision. Every defect image differs from it by exactly the recorded edits.

defects.description: Rollback compensates completed steps in forward order instead of reverse order, so later side effects are undone before the earlier state they depend on is restored.

The transaction-wide timeout is measured from each step's start instead of the transaction start, so a transaction whose steps individually fit the budget never times out no matter how long it runs in total.

edits.find:
const elapsed = this.startTime ? Date.now() - this.startTime : 0;
      const remaining = this.options.timeout - elapsed;
edits.replace:
const elapsed = 0;
      const remaining = this.options.timeout - elapsed;

defects.description: A rolled-back transaction accepts new steps instead of rejecting them, so callers can keep appending work to a transaction whose earlier effects were already compensated.
Errors thrown by compensation functions during rollback are silently discarded, so a partially failed rollback reports the original step error and never surfaces CompensationFailedError.
A step given an already-aborted external signal still executes: the pre-abort check is replaced by a listener that never fires for signals aborted before registration.

Two steps can run concurrently in one transaction: the in-flight guard only triggers in a state that never coincides with a running step, so overlapping run calls share and clobber the abort controller.
A rolled-back transaction can still be committed, so callers observe a transaction that both compensated its work and reports a successful commit.
RetryExhaustedError carries only the final attempt's error instead of the full per-attempt history, so debugging output and error consumers lose every earlier failure cause.
Successful steps are not counted as completed, so a later failure rolls back nothing and every completed side effect survives the reported rollback.
Route allow-listing matches by prefix instead of exact pathname, so a policy for /checkout also authorizes snapshot capture on unrelated routes like /checkout-admin.
The snapshot age comparison is inverted, so snapshots older than the TTL are kept forever and stale content keeps being prepainted.
The size limit compares UTF-16 string length instead of encoded UTF-8 bytes, so multibyte snapshots far above maxSnapshotBytes are kept.

edits.find: if (getSnapshotPayloadBytes(snapshot as Snapshot) > policy.maxSnapshotBytes) return true;

defects.description: The staleness comparison is inverted: data older than the ttl reports fresh and freshly updated data reports stale, so revalidation runs at exactly the wrong times.
The combined-snapshot memo check ignores history changes, so a history-only update (for example a conflict flag) returns the previous cached snapshot and consumers never see it.
CacheManager.subscribe returns an unsubscribe that removes nothing, so detached consumers keep receiving updates and the subscriber set grows for the model's lifetime.
Subscribers are not notified when the cache enters the error state, so consumers keep rendering the previous loading or success state after a failure.
Policy validation accepts relative route strings, so a policy like routes: ['home'] silently becomes active instead of being rejected, and capture decisions run against malformed route keys.
A tab reacts to its own broadcast messages: the sender-id filter is removed, so every local mutation also triggers the local refresh callbacks as if another tab had changed the model.
Unsubscribing one listener silently removes every listener registered for the same model key, so remaining subscribers stop receiving cross-tab updates.
Retry exhausts one attempt early: a step configured with maxAttempts N gives up after N-1 tries, so work that would succeed on the final attempt is reported as exhausted.
